claim: Paying 1 point to go from 7% to 6.75% cuts the payment by $16.7 per $100,000 borrowed, so the point takes 59.9 months (about five years) to pay for itself. Across 2,635 start weeks of the weekly 30-year rate since April 1971, the market rate fell at least 1.25 points (enough to make a refinance from 6.75% worthwhile by the common one-point rule) before that break-even in 53.1% of weeks; when it did, the median wait was 18.9 months. Restricting to weeks that started between 6.5% and 7.5% (362 weeks) gives 52.2%. The latest weekly rate is 7.03%. History, not a forecast.

numbers.definition: Level monthly payment for a 360-month loan: p*x/(1-(1+x)^-360), x = rate/1200. Payment at 7.00% minus payment at 6.75% on $100,000, rounded to cents.
Level monthly payment for a 360-month loan: p*x/(1-(1+x)^-360), x = rate/1200. Point cost (1% of the loan) divided by the monthly payment saving (scale-free: 1.0 / saving per $100), rounded to 0.1.
breakeven_months rounded up to a whole month (ceil of the unrounded value).

Data: data/MORTGAGE30US.csv (FRED MORTGAGE30US, 30-Year Fixed Rate Mortgage Average in the United States, weekly, percent), all weeks 1971-04-02 through 2026-09-24, rates converted to integer hundredths. For each week t, horizon end = same calendar day 60 months later (clipped to month end); weeks whose horizon end is after 2026-09-24 are excluded. A week counts as a hit if any later week w with t < w <= horizon end has rate(w) <= rate(t) - 1.25 points (i.e. the market fell 1.00 point below the 6.75% bought-down note rate, measured from a start rate 0.25 above it). Number of eligible start weeks.

assumptions: One point costs 1% of the loan and lowers the rate by 0.25 (7.00% to 6.75%) on a 30-year fixed loan; simple (undiscounted) break-even.
Refinance trigger: the weekly average 30-year rate at least 1.00 point below the borrower's note rate; closing costs and the borrower's own rate spread vs the survey average are ignored.
The no-point rate equals the survey rate in the start week; history is applied as point changes from that week's rate.
A hit means the refinance opportunity appeared; it does not assume the borrower took it or quantify how much of the point was lost.
